**Michigan Stadium**, nicknamed "**The Big House**,"[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michigan_Stadium#cite_note-7) is the American footballstadium for the University of Michigan in Ann Arbor, Michigan. It is the largest stadium in the United States and the Western Hemisphere, the third-largest stadium in the world, and the 34th-largest sports venue in the world.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michigan_Stadium#cite_note-size-8)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michigan_Stadium#cite_note-9) Its official capacity is 107,601, but it has hosted crowds in excess of 115,000.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michigan_Stadium#cite_note-10)
Michigan Stadium was designed with footings to allow the stadium's capacity to be expanded beyond 100,000.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michigan_Stadium#cite_note-:0-11)Fielding Yost envisioned a day where 150,000 seats would be needed.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michigan_Stadium#cite_note-:0-11) To keep construction costs low at the time, the decision was made to build a smaller stadium than Yost envisioned but to include the footings for future expansion.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michigan_Stadium#cite_note-maxsize-12)

Michigan Stadium is used for the University of Michigan's main graduation ceremonies; PresidentLyndon B. Johnson outlined his Great Society program at the 1964 commencement ceremonies in the stadium.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michigan_Stadium#cite_note-13) It has also hosted ice hockey games including the 2014 NHL Winter Classic, a regular season NHL game between the Toronto Maple Leafs and the Detroit Red Wings with an official attendance of 105,491, a record for an ice hockey game.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michigan_Stadium#cite_note-lage-14) Additionally, a 2014 International Champions Cup soccer match between Real Madrid and Manchester United had an attendance of 109,318, a record for a soccer match in the United States.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michigan_Stadium#cite_note-ICC-15)

### Construction and early years
[edit]
Michigan Stadium was built in 1927 at a cost of $950,000 (equivalent to $14.1 million in 2025[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michigan_Stadium#cite_note-inflation-USGDP-5)) and had an original capacity of 72,000. Prior to the stadium's construction, the Wolverines played football at Ferry Field. Every home game since November 8, 1975 has drawn a crowd in excess of 100,000, an active streak of more than 300 contests.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michigan_Stadium#cite_note-history-16) On September 7, 2013, the game between Michigan and the Notre Dame Fighting Irish attracted a crowd of 115,109, a record attendance for a college football game since 1948, and an NCAA single-game attendance record at the time, overtaking the previous record of 114,804 set two years previously for the same matchup.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michigan_Stadium#cite_note-NCAA_att-17)
The dedication of Michigan Stadium on October 22, 1927, prior to Michigan's game against Ohio State

### Construction and early years
Prior to playing at Michigan Stadium, Michigan played its games at Ferry Field, which at its peak could seat 40,000 people. Fielding Yost recognized the need for a larger stadium after original expansions to Ferry Field proved to be too small, and persuaded the regents to build a permanent stadium in 1926. Fashioned after the Yale Bowl, the original stadium was built with a capacity of 72,000, though Yost originally wanted to have a capacity of 140,000.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michigan_Stadium#cite_note-18) At Yost's urging, temporary bleachers were added at the top of the stadium, increasing capacity to 82,000.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michigan_Stadium#cite_note-history-16)[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michigan_Stadium#cite_note-expansion-19)
On October 1, 1927, Michigan played Ohio Wesleyan in the first game at Michigan Stadium, prevailing easily, 33–0. The new stadium was then formally dedicated three weeks later in a contest against Ohio State on October 22. Michigan had spoiled the formal dedication of Ohio Stadium in Columbus five years earlier and was victorious again, besting the Buckeyes 21–0 before a standing-room-only crowd of 84,401. In 1930, electronic scoreboards were installed, making the stadium the first in the United States to use them to keep the official game time.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michigan_Stadium#cite_note-history-16)
In 1956, the addition of a press box raised the stadium's official capacity to 101,001. The one "extra seat" in Michigan Stadium is said to be reserved for Fritz Crisler, athletic director at the time.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michigan_Stadium#cite_note-crisler-20) Since then, all official Michigan Stadium capacity figures have ended in "-01", although the extra seat's location is not specified.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michigan_Stadium#cite_note-history-16)

### Construction and early years
Before 1968, Michigan Stadium maintained a policy of "No women or children allowed on the field". Sara Krulwich, now a photojournalist for _The New York Times_, was the first woman on the field.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michigan_Stadium#cite_note-Essay-21) Longtime radio announcer Bob Ufer dubbed Michigan Stadium "The hole that Yost dug, Crisler paid for, Canham carpeted, and Schembechler fills every cotton-pickin' Saturday afternoon".[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michigan_Stadium#cite_note-Feldman-22) Since November 8, 1975, the stadium has held over 100,000 fans for every home game (the Indiana University contest on October 25, 1975 attracted "only" 93,857 fans).[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michigan_Stadium#cite_note-MUAtt1-23)[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michigan_Stadium#cite_note-1975_team-24)—and 24 of the 25 most attended NCAA games are at the stadium.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michigan_Stadium#cite_note-NCAA_att-17) Michigan Stadium's size is not wholly apparent from the outside as most of the seats are below ground level.
By the mid-1980s, Michigan Stadium had become known by the nickname "The Big House", with Keith Jackson credited for popularizing the nickname.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michigan_Stadium#cite_note-25)[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michigan_Stadium#cite_note-26)[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michigan_Stadium#cite_note-27)[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michigan_Stadium#cite_note-28)
The west side structure at Michigan Stadium

### Construction and early years
Michigan's game versus Ball State University on November 4, 2006, was the 200th consecutive crowd of over 100,000 fans.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michigan_Stadium#cite_note-200th_Game-29) When the game's attendance is announced, the public address announcer, historically Howard King, thanks the fans for "being part of the largest crowd watching a football game anywhere in America today".[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michigan_Stadium#cite_note-Centered-30)
On September 9, 2006, attendees of Michigan's football game against the Central Michigan Chippewas endured the first weather delay in the stadium's history after lightning struck nearby during the first quarter and play was suspended for approximately one hour.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michigan_Stadium#cite_note-LATimes-31)
On September 3, 2011, Michigan and Western Michigan mutually agreed to end their game with 1:27 left in the third quarter because of an ongoing lightning delay. It was the first time Michigan had a football game called because of lightning. The stadium was evacuated at 6:38 p.m. and the game was called shortly after 7:00.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michigan_Stadium#cite_note-knight-32)
On June 21, 2007, the University's Board of Regents approved a $226 million renovation (equivalent to $338 million in 2025[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michigan_Stadium#cite_note-inflation-USGDP-5)) and expansion project for Michigan Stadium. The project included replacement of some bleachers, widening of aisles and individual seats, installing hand rails, and the addition of a new press box, 83 luxury boxes, and 3,200 club seats. The renovation plan garnered opposition from a small number of students, alumni, and fans around the country, which waned as the renovation neared external completion.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michigan_Stadium#cite_note-AAnews-33)

## Seating and surface
With an attendance of 104,173, "The Big Chill at the Big House" set the record attendance for a hockey game.[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michigan_Stadium#cite_note-guinness-55) The record was broken on January 1, 2014 for the NHL's 2014 Winter Classic, where a crowd of 105,491 saw the host Detroit Red Wings fall to the Toronto Maple Leafs in a shootout.
On Saturday, August 2, 2014, a sell-out crowd of 109,318 watched [Manchester United](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manchester_United_F.C. "Manchester United F.C.") defeat [Real Madrid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Real_Madrid_C.F. "Real Madrid C.F.") 3-1 in an International Champions Cup match.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michigan_Stadium#cite_note-56) The official attendance figure was the largest for a soccer game in the United States to date, overtaking the previous record set by the 1984 Olympics Gold Medal match, when 101,799 saw France defeat Brazil 2-0 at the Rose Bowl in Pasadena, California.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michigan_Stadium#cite_note-ICC-15)[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michigan_Stadium#cite_note-57) Michigan Stadium also holds three of the top four U.S. Soccer attendances as a crowd of 105,826 watched a 2016 International Champions Cup match on July 30, 2016 where Real Madrid defeated [Chelsea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chelsea_F.C. "Chelsea F.C.") 3-2 and a crowd of 101,254 watched a 2018 International Champions Cup match on July 28, 2018 where [Liverpool](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liverpool_F.C. "Liverpool F.C.") defeated Manchester United 4-1.

## Seating and surface
On February 12, 2025, the University of Michigan Athletic Department and multi-Platinum, GRAMMY-winning artist Zach Bryan jointly announced a first-of-its-kind concert at Michigan Stadium on Sept. 27, 2025, with special guest John Mayer. Ryan Bingham and The Texas Gentlemen and Joshua Slone will also be joining the bill for Michigan Stadium's inaugural dedicated concert[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michigan_Stadium#cite_note-58)
That concert subsequently broke the record for largest attendance ever at a U.S. ticketed concert with a single headlining act. He played to an announced crowd of 112,408, breaking the previous record set by George Strait on Saturday, June 15, 2024, with a concert at Kyle Field at Texas A&M University in College Station, Texas, with 110,905 fans in attendance.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michigan_Stadium#cite_note-59) It was only the second concert in the 98-year history of the venue, but the first by a headlining act.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michigan_Stadium#cite_note-60)

**Michigan Stadium**, nicknamed "**The Big House**,"[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michigan_Stadium#cite_note-7) is the American footballstadium for the University of Michigan in Ann Arbor, Michigan. It is the largest stadium in the United States and the Western Hemisphere, the third-largest stadium in the world, and the 34th-largest sports venue in the world.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michigan_Stadium#cite_note-size-8)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michigan_Stadium#cite_note-9) Its official capacity is 107,601, but it has hosted crowds in excess of 115,000.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michigan_Stadium#cite_note-10)
Michigan Stadium was designed with footings to allow the stadium's capacity to be expanded beyond 100,000.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michigan_Stadium#cite_note-:0-11)Fielding Yost envisioned a day where 150,000 seats would be needed.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michigan_Stadium#cite_note-:0-11) To keep construction costs low at the time, the decision was made to build a smaller stadium than Yost envisioned but to include the footings for future expansion.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michigan_Stadium#cite_note-maxsize-12)
texts.3: Michigan Stadium is used for the University of Michigan's main graduation ceremonies; PresidentLyndon B. Johnson outlined his Great Society program at the 1964 commencement ceremonies in the stadium.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michigan_Stadium#cite_note-13) It has also hosted ice hockey games including the 2014 NHL Winter Classic, a regular season NHL game between the Toronto Maple Leafs and the Detroit Red Wings with an official attendance of 105,491, a record for an ice hockey game.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michigan_Stadium#cite_note-lage-14) Additionally, a 2014 International Champions Cup soccer match between Real Madrid and Manchester United had an attendance of 109,318, a record for a soccer match in the United States.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michigan_Stadium#cite_note-ICC-15)

### Construction and early years
[edit]
Michigan Stadium was built in 1927 at a cost of $950,000 (equivalent to $14.1 million in 2025[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michigan_Stadium#cite_note-inflation-USGDP-5)) and had an original capacity of 72,000. Prior to the stadium's construction, the Wolverines played football at Ferry Field. Every home game since November 8, 1975 has drawn a crowd in excess of 100,000, an active streak of more than 300 contests.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michigan_Stadium#cite_note-history-16) On September 7, 2013, the game between Michigan and the Notre Dame Fighting Irish attracted a crowd of 115,109, a record attendance for a college football game since 1948, and an NCAA single-game attendance record at the time, overtaking the previous record of 114,804 set two years previously for the same matchup.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michigan_Stadium#cite_note-NCAA_att-17)
The dedication of Michigan Stadium on October 22, 1927, prior to Michigan's game against Ohio State

### Construction and early years
Prior to playing at Michigan Stadium, Michigan played its games at Ferry Field, which at its peak could seat 40,000 people. Fielding Yost recognized the need for a larger stadium after original expansions to Ferry Field proved to be too small, and persuaded the regents to build a permanent stadium in 1926. Fashioned after the Yale Bowl, the original stadium was built with a capacity of 72,000, though Yost originally wanted to have a capacity of 140,000.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michigan_Stadium#cite_note-18) At Yost's urging, temporary bleachers were added at the top of the stadium, increasing capacity to 82,000.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michigan_Stadium#cite_note-history-16)[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michigan_Stadium#cite_note-expansion-19)
On October 1, 1927, Michigan played Ohio Wesleyan in the first game at Michigan Stadium, prevailing easily, 33–0. The new stadium was then formally dedicated three weeks later in a contest against Ohio State on October 22. Michigan had spoiled the formal dedication of Ohio Stadium in Columbus five years earlier and was victorious again, besting the Buckeyes 21–0 before a standing-room-only crowd of 84,401. In 1930, electronic scoreboards were installed, making the stadium the first in the United States to use them to keep the official game time.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michigan_Stadium#cite_note-history-16)
In 1956, the addition of a press box raised the stadium's official capacity to 101,001. The one "extra seat" in Michigan Stadium is said to be reserved for Fritz Crisler, athletic director at the time.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michigan_Stadium#cite_note-crisler-20) Since then, all official Michigan Stadium capacity figures have ended in "-01", although the extra seat's location is not specified.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michigan_Stadium#cite_note-history-16)

### Construction and early years
Before 1968, Michigan Stadium maintained a policy of "No women or children allowed on the field". Sara Krulwich, now a photojournalist for _The New York Times_, was the first woman on the field.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michigan_Stadium#cite_note-Essay-21) Longtime radio announcer Bob Ufer dubbed Michigan Stadium "The hole that Yost dug, Crisler paid for, Canham carpeted, and Schembechler fills every cotton-pickin' Saturday afternoon".[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michigan_Stadium#cite_note-Feldman-22) Since November 8, 1975, the stadium has held over 100,000 fans for every home game (the Indiana University contest on October 25, 1975 attracted "only" 93,857 fans).[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michigan_Stadium#cite_note-MUAtt1-23)[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michigan_Stadium#cite_note-1975_team-24)—and 24 of the 25 most attended NCAA games are at the stadium.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michigan_Stadium#cite_note-NCAA_att-17) Michigan Stadium's size is not wholly apparent from the outside as most of the seats are below ground level.
By the mid-1980s, Michigan Stadium had become known by the nickname "The Big House", with Keith Jackson credited for popularizing the nickname.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michigan_Stadium#cite_note-25)[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michigan_Stadium#cite_note-26)[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michigan_Stadium#cite_note-27)[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michigan_Stadium#cite_note-28)
The west side structure at Michigan Stadium

### Construction and early years
Michigan's game versus Ball State University on November 4, 2006, was the 200th consecutive crowd of over 100,000 fans.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michigan_Stadium#cite_note-200th_Game-29) When the game's attendance is announced, the public address announcer, historically Howard King, thanks the fans for "being part of the largest crowd watching a football game anywhere in America today".[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michigan_Stadium#cite_note-Centered-30)
On September 9, 2006, attendees of Michigan's football game against the Central Michigan Chippewas endured the first weather delay in the stadium's history after lightning struck nearby during the first quarter and play was suspended for approximately one hour.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michigan_Stadium#cite_note-LATimes-31)
On September 3, 2011, Michigan and Western Michigan mutually agreed to end their game with 1:27 left in the third quarter because of an ongoing lightning delay. It was the first time Michigan had a football game called because of lightning. The stadium was evacuated at 6:38 p.m. and the game was called shortly after 7:00.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michigan_Stadium#cite_note-knight-32)
On June 21, 2007, the University's Board of Regents approved a $226 million renovation (equivalent to $338 million in 2025[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michigan_Stadium#cite_note-inflation-USGDP-5)) and expansion project for Michigan Stadium. The project included replacement of some bleachers, widening of aisles and individual seats, installing hand rails, and the addition of a new press box, 83 luxury boxes, and 3,200 club seats. The renovation plan garnered opposition from a small number of students, alumni, and fans around the country, which waned as the renovation neared external completion.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michigan_Stadium#cite_note-AAnews-33)

## Seating and surface
With an attendance of 104,173, "The Big Chill at the Big House" set the record attendance for a hockey game.[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michigan_Stadium#cite_note-guinness-55) The record was broken on January 1, 2014 for the NHL's 2014 Winter Classic, where a crowd of 105,491 saw the host Detroit Red Wings fall to the Toronto Maple Leafs in a shootout.
On Saturday, August 2, 2014, a sell-out crowd of 109,318 watched [Manchester United](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manchester_United_F.C. "Manchester United F.C.") defeat [Real Madrid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Real_Madrid_C.F. "Real Madrid C.F.") 3-1 in an International Champions Cup match.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michigan_Stadium#cite_note-56) The official attendance figure was the largest for a soccer game in the United States to date, overtaking the previous record set by the 1984 Olympics Gold Medal match, when 101,799 saw France defeat Brazil 2-0 at the Rose Bowl in Pasadena, California.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michigan_Stadium#cite_note-ICC-15)[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michigan_Stadium#cite_note-57) Michigan Stadium also holds three of the top four U.S. Soccer attendances as a crowd of 105,826 watched a 2016 International Champions Cup match on July 30, 2016 where Real Madrid defeated [Chelsea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chelsea_F.C. "Chelsea F.C.") 3-2 and a crowd of 101,254 watched a 2018 International Champions Cup match on July 28, 2018 where [Liverpool](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liverpool_F.C. "Liverpool F.C.") defeated Manchester United 4-1.

## Seating and surface
On February 12, 2025, the University of Michigan Athletic Department and multi-Platinum, GRAMMY-winning artist Zach Bryan jointly announced a first-of-its-kind concert at Michigan Stadium on Sept. 27, 2025, with special guest John Mayer. Ryan Bingham and The Texas Gentlemen and Joshua Slone will also be joining the bill for Michigan Stadium's inaugural dedicated concert[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michigan_Stadium#cite_note-58)
That concert subsequently broke the record for largest attendance ever at a U.S. ticketed concert with a single headlining act. He played to an announced crowd of 112,408, breaking the previous record set by George Strait on Saturday, June 15, 2024, with a concert at Kyle Field at Texas A&M University in College Station, Texas, with 110,905 fans in attendance.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michigan_Stadium#cite_note-59) It was only the second concert in the 98-year history of the venue, but the first by a headlining act.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michigan_Stadium#cite_note-60)

**Michigan Stadium**, nicknamed "**The Big House**,"[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michigan_Stadium#cite_note-7) is the American footballstadium for the University of Michigan in Ann Arbor, Michigan. It is the largest stadium in the United States and the Western Hemisphere, the third-largest stadium in the world, and the 34th-largest sports venue in the world.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michigan_Stadium#cite_note-size-8)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michigan_Stadium#cite_note-9) Its official capacity is 107,601, but it has hosted crowds in excess of 115,000.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michigan_Stadium#cite_note-10)
Michigan Stadium was designed with footings to allow the stadium's capacity to be expanded beyond 100,000.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michigan_Stadium#cite_note-:0-11)Fielding Yost envisioned a day where 150,000 seats would be needed.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michigan_Stadium#cite_note-:0-11) To keep construction costs low at the time, the decision was made to build a smaller stadium than Yost envisioned but to include the footings for future expansion.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michigan_Stadium#cite_note-maxsize-12)

Michigan Stadium is used for the University of Michigan's main graduation ceremonies; PresidentLyndon B. Johnson outlined his Great Society program at the 1964 commencement ceremonies in the stadium.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michigan_Stadium#cite_note-13) It has also hosted ice hockey games including the 2014 NHL Winter Classic, a regular season NHL game between the Toronto Maple Leafs and the Detroit Red Wings with an official attendance of 105,491, a record for an ice hockey game.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michigan_Stadium#cite_note-lage-14) Additionally, a 2014 International Champions Cup soccer match between Real Madrid and Manchester United had an attendance of 109,318, a record for a soccer match in the United States.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michigan_Stadium#cite_note-ICC-15)

### Construction and early years
[edit]
Michigan Stadium was built in 1927 at a cost of $950,000 (equivalent to $14.1 million in 2025[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michigan_Stadium#cite_note-inflation-USGDP-5)) and had an original capacity of 72,000. Prior to the stadium's construction, the Wolverines played football at Ferry Field. Every home game since November 8, 1975 has drawn a crowd in excess of 100,000, an active streak of more than 300 contests.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michigan_Stadium#cite_note-history-16) On September 7, 2013, the game between Michigan and the Notre Dame Fighting Irish attracted a crowd of 115,109, a record attendance for a college football game since 1948, and an NCAA single-game attendance record at the time, overtaking the previous record of 114,804 set two years previously for the same matchup.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michigan_Stadium#cite_note-NCAA_att-17)
The dedication of Michigan Stadium on October 22, 1927, prior to Michigan's game against Ohio State

### Construction and early years
Prior to playing at Michigan Stadium, Michigan played its games at Ferry Field, which at its peak could seat 40,000 people. Fielding Yost recognized the need for a larger stadium after original expansions to Ferry Field proved to be too small, and persuaded the regents to build a permanent stadium in 1926. Fashioned after the Yale Bowl, the original stadium was built with a capacity of 72,000, though Yost originally wanted to have a capacity of 140,000.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michigan_Stadium#cite_note-18) At Yost's urging, temporary bleachers were added at the top of the stadium, increasing capacity to 82,000.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michigan_Stadium#cite_note-history-16)[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michigan_Stadium#cite_note-expansion-19)
On October 1, 1927, Michigan played Ohio Wesleyan in the first game at Michigan Stadium, prevailing easily, 33–0. The new stadium was then formally dedicated three weeks later in a contest against Ohio State on October 22. Michigan had spoiled the formal dedication of Ohio Stadium in Columbus five years earlier and was victorious again, besting the Buckeyes 21–0 before a standing-room-only crowd of 84,401. In 1930, electronic scoreboards were installed, making the stadium the first in the United States to use them to keep the official game time.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michigan_Stadium#cite_note-history-16)
In 1956, the addition of a press box raised the stadium's official capacity to 101,001. The one "extra seat" in Michigan Stadium is said to be reserved for Fritz Crisler, athletic director at the time.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michigan_Stadium#cite_note-crisler-20) Since then, all official Michigan Stadium capacity figures have ended in "-01", although the extra seat's location is not specified.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michigan_Stadium#cite_note-history-16)

### Construction and early years
Before 1968, Michigan Stadium maintained a policy of "No women or children allowed on the field". Sara Krulwich, now a photojournalist for _The New York Times_, was the first woman on the field.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michigan_Stadium#cite_note-Essay-21) Longtime radio announcer Bob Ufer dubbed Michigan Stadium "The hole that Yost dug, Crisler paid for, Canham carpeted, and Schembechler fills every cotton-pickin' Saturday afternoon".[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michigan_Stadium#cite_note-Feldman-22) Since November 8, 1975, the stadium has held over 100,000 fans for every home game (the Indiana University contest on October 25, 1975 attracted "only" 93,857 fans).[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michigan_Stadium#cite_note-MUAtt1-23)[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michigan_Stadium#cite_note-1975_team-24)—and 24 of the 25 most attended NCAA games are at the stadium.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michigan_Stadium#cite_note-NCAA_att-17) Michigan Stadium's size is not wholly apparent from the outside as most of the seats are below ground level.
By the mid-1980s, Michigan Stadium had become known by the nickname "The Big House", with Keith Jackson credited for popularizing the nickname.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michigan_Stadium#cite_note-25)[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michigan_Stadium#cite_note-26)[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michigan_Stadium#cite_note-27)[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michigan_Stadium#cite_note-28)
The west side structure at Michigan Stadium

### Construction and early years
Michigan's game versus Ball State University on November 4, 2006, was the 200th consecutive crowd of over 100,000 fans.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michigan_Stadium#cite_note-200th_Game-29) When the game's attendance is announced, the public address announcer, historically Howard King, thanks the fans for "being part of the largest crowd watching a football game anywhere in America today".[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michigan_Stadium#cite_note-Centered-30)
On September 9, 2006, attendees of Michigan's football game against the Central Michigan Chippewas endured the first weather delay in the stadium's history after lightning struck nearby during the first quarter and play was suspended for approximately one hour.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michigan_Stadium#cite_note-LATimes-31)
On September 3, 2011, Michigan and Western Michigan mutually agreed to end their game with 1:27 left in the third quarter because of an ongoing lightning delay. It was the first time Michigan had a football game called because of lightning. The stadium was evacuated at 6:38 p.m. and the game was called shortly after 7:00.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michigan_Stadium#cite_note-knight-32)
On June 21, 2007, the University's Board of Regents approved a $226 million renovation (equivalent to $338 million in 2025[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michigan_Stadium#cite_note-inflation-USGDP-5)) and expansion project for Michigan Stadium. The project included replacement of some bleachers, widening of aisles and individual seats, installing hand rails, and the addition of a new press box, 83 luxury boxes, and 3,200 club seats. The renovation plan garnered opposition from a small number of students, alumni, and fans around the country, which waned as the renovation neared external completion.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michigan_Stadium#cite_note-AAnews-33)
